rv.q: No worry here; “Sondheim on Sondheim” is engrossingly entertaining and thoroughly captivating.
The evening has the feel of a classroom discussion in which the professor happens to be a genius and the students happen to be among the finest Broadway performers of their generation.
This somewhat jittery production never quite finds a sustained tone, a natural rhythm or even a logical sense of sequence.
Too much of a good thing can be wonderful – but could be even more wonderful with ruthless editing to prevent a sense at the finish of “10 minutes too long”.
Any show in which Ms. Cook sings "Loving You," "Take Me to the World" and "Send in the Clowns" is by definition worth seeing.
But basically, it’s an entertainment for hard-core Sondheim fanatics who would rather hear the Ethel Merman song that was cut from “Gypsy” than the classic numbers that remain.
One would love to report that the performances were as transforming as the documentary.
Indeed, even with such skilled interpreters as Barbara Cook and Vanessa Williams on board, the numbers flatline.
The resulting show is wise, warm, witty, and entirely wonderful.

Sondheim's words and music are, for all their intelligence and sophistication, most striking for their emotional fidelity to his characters and the universal struggles and joys informing their disparate journeys.
But she doesn't fit into a revue.
Despite multimedia razzle-dazzle and clever medleys, “Sondheim on Sondheim” is best, sadly, in its prerecorded bits.
The word 'disappointing' firmly stuck in my head.
It’s a pleasure to see him narrate the artistic trajectory of his life and work with the same panache that animates his memorable shows.
"Sondheim on Sondheim" is polished and well-intentioned, but it leaves you hungry for something more substantial and involving.

cn.t: Critics find this Sondheim retrospective enjoyable but uneven, with Lapine's innovative video integration and stellar performers (especially Barbara Cook) elevating material that sometimes feels wan or schizophrenic onstage.
